summary:
Zimbabwe criminalises same-sex sexual activity between men and between women. The Human Dignity Trust country profile records that the offence covers sodomy and, for conduct between males, acts that would be regarded by a reasonable person as indecent, so contact short of intercourse can still fall within the criminal law.

Amnesty International's report of 9 January 2024 (index AFR 01/7533/2024), 'We are facing extinction — escalating anti-LGBTI sentiment, the weaponisation of law and their human rights implications in select African countries', examines anti-LGBTI sentiment and the use of law against LGBTI people in the countries it selects, Zimbabwe among them. Its finding of law deployed as an instrument of hostility is the operative risk context a visitor faces alongside the statutory exposure itself.

Healthcare access is formally protected. In July 2018 the health ministry released a 68-page training handbook for all health practitioners on serving gay people, sex workers and transgender or non-gender-conforming people in public health institutions. The manual states that care for these groups is legal and every provider's duty, recording that nowhere in policy or law makes it illegal to provide healthcare services to members of key population groups. It was issued because patients had avoided clinics fearing mistreatment or police tip-offs by staff. For a trans visitor this means formal policy guarantees health-service access, including transition-relevant care at public facilities, while day-to-day treatment depends on staff trained under a 2018 handbook.

Support machinery remains reachable despite criminalisation. GALZ (Gays and Lesbians of Zimbabwe), a voluntary membership organisation established in 1990, reports more than 4,000 community members, 35 years of advocacy, 10 affinity groups and 4 resource centres, with services covering legal support that explicitly includes arrests for 'sodomy', counselling, hospital-fee assistance and empowerment programmes for LGBTI Zimbabweans. Legal aid and counselling are therefore available to an LGBTI traveller.
tangentialFactors:
Prejudice shapes everyday conduct independently of prosecution. A 2012 social work study, Mabvurira et al. in the International Journal of Humanities and Social Science, reports that homosexual Zimbabweans live secluded lives because of prejudice, and argues that homosexuality is 'as African as the baobab tree and as Zimbabwean as the Great Zimbabwe Ruins', tracing same-sex relations in pre-colonial and post-colonial Zimbabwe while urging social workers to promote social justice for the gay community. The paper is academic advocacy rather than law, but it evidences the social climate a visitor enters.

The 2018 handbook was prompted by reported avoidance of clinics over fear of mistreatment and of staff reporting patients to police, which indicates that the risk of being outed in a medical setting predates and outlasts the policy response. Formal guarantees and reported practice diverge.

Published academic work on homosexuality in Zimbabwe exists in the wider literature, including an article in the Journal of Homosexuality, but it does not address trans-specific legal questions.
localsOnly:
GALZ functions as the principal resident-facing support structure: a voluntary membership body founded in 1990 with more than 4,000 community members, 10 affinity groups and 4 resource centres, delivering legal support that expressly covers arrests for 'sodomy', counselling, hospital-fee assistance and empowerment programmes for LGBTI Zimbabweans.

The health ministry's 68-page handbook binds all health practitioners serving key population groups in public health institutions and frames provision of care as a professional duty, so residents can invoke it when refused service. Its issuance followed reports that patients were staying away from clinics.

Professional social work in Zimbabwe carries an articulated obligation to promote social justice for the gay community, per the 2012 Mabvurira et al. study, though this is a professional-ethics position rather than an enforceable entitlement.
outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory does not state the statutory penalties attaching to the sodomy and indecent-contact offences, nor whether they are enforced; prosecution frequency and recent case law are not sourced here.

No source in the inventory addresses legal gender recognition, amendment of sex markers on passports or identity documents, visa and border-screening questions that risk disclosure of gender history, or facilities and bathroom access. These remain unresolved and are not sourced.

Hate-crime provisions, anti-discrimination protections covering gender identity, and recognition of partners or marriages are likewise not covered by the available sources.

The current status of the July 2018 handbook, the proportion of practitioners actually trained under it, and whether it remains in force under later health-ministry administrations are unverified. The academic sources date from 2010 and 2012 and are not confirmed as describing present conditions.
